metadata.title: From asking to observing. Behavioural measures of socio-emotional and motivational skills in large-scale assessments

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA’s two-stage stratified sampling design for 15-year-old students and applies PISA sampling and replication weights “in line with recommended PISA procedures (OECD, 2014)”. The analytic sample is restricted to students with non-missing values for the PSEC indicators and (where relevant) the control variables used in each model specification, and for some behavioural indicators additional item-level inclusion rules are applied (e.g., at least 3 non-missing responses within a scale). For the achievement–PSEC association models, the authors include country fixed effects and, in extended specifications, student background controls (grade, age, gender, SES, immigrant background, and language background). The manuscript does not report the exact weight variable names or the replicate-weight method (e.g., BRR/Fay), but it explicitly states that sampling and replication weights were used, implying complex-survey variance estimation consistent with PISA guidance.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper does not report a plausible-values (PV) strategy because the dependent variables are behavioural indicators derived from questionnaire responses and test-taking behaviour (e.g., item non-response, inconsistency, non-differentiation, performance decline, response-time effort) and binary educational attainment outcomes in longitudinal follow-ups. These outcomes are not PV-based cognitive achievement scores, so PV handling is not applicable. For missing data, the authors state that models include students with non-missing values for all PSEC indicators and controls, but they do not explicitly describe whether missingness was handled via listwise deletion, pairwise deletion, or any imputation procedure; therefore the missing-data handling is not fully documented.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Most analyses are based on PISA 2012, using the core student questionnaire and (for a subset of countries) computer-based assessment log files. The paper-based behavioural indicators are constructed from questionnaire items with specific inclusion rules (e.g., dropped conditional items; for inconsistency and non-differentiation, respondents must have non-missing responses for at least 3 items within a scale/item set; non-differentiation uses item sets with at least 4 items). For the test-based behavioural indicator of performance decline, the authors use only the first three clusters to reduce end-of-test non-response bias and estimate a random-coefficient model separately by country, then use BLUPs of the random slope. For response-time effort, they use computer-based assessment log files and compute the proportion of items with response times below thresholds (reported mainly for 5s). For the longitudinal predictive validity analyses, the sample is restricted to the subset of countries with follow-up data (Denmark, Switzerland, Australia, Canada) and to students with non-missing values for the PSEC indicators and controls used in each linear probability model.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 (15-year-olds) — paper-based assessment (reading, mathematics, science, collaborative problem-solving)
main_findings.target_variable: Contemporaneous achievement (reading, math, science, collaborative problem-solving) associated with PSEC indicators
top_predictors: Self-reported lack of effort in test
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 3: standardized regression coefficients (b) with significance and adjusted R-squared. Example magnitudes (Model B, with background controls): self-reported lack of perseverance b≈−0.11 (reading), −0.13 (math), −0.11 (science), −0.10 (collaborative problem-solving); non-response b≈−0.27 (reading/math/science) and −0.27 (collaborative problem-solving). Adjusted R-squared ranges by indicator/model (e.g., non-response Model B adjusted R-squared ≈0.21 for collaborative problem-solving).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 the study leveraged self-reported perseverance/effort and questionnaire-based behavioural indicators (non-response, non-differentiation, inconsistency) to predict contemporaneous achievement in reading, mathematics, science, and collaborative problem-solving, finding that all PSEC indicators were negatively associated with achievement and that the strongest behavioural association came from item non-response. This indicates that behavioural engagement/response-quality signals captured during low-stakes testing can provide policy-relevant information about students’ learning readiness beyond self-reports, though the study is correlational and does not establish causal effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 (15-year-olds) — paper-based assessment (reading, mathematics, science, collaborative problem-solving)
main_findings.target_variable: Contemporaneous achievement associated with test-based behavioural indicators (performance decline, response-time effort)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 3: Model A vs B vs C coefficients. Example (Model B, with background controls): performance decline b≈−0.13 (reading), −0.12 (math), −0.12 (science), −0.15 (collaborative problem-solving). Response time effort (5s) Model B: b≈−0.15 (reading), −0.13 (math), −0.12 (science), −0.20 (collaborative problem-solving). Model C (adding self-reported perseverance/effort) shows coefficients remain negative and significant (e.g., performance decline collaborative problem-solving b≈−0.14, sig=***; response time effort (5s) collaborative problem-solving b≈−0.19, sig=***).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 the study leveraged test-based behavioural indicators—performance decline and response-time effort—to predict contemporaneous achievement across all PISA domains, finding that both indicators were consistently negatively associated with achievement and that the associations remained robust after adding self-reported perseverance/effort. This indicates that task-based behavioural measures can complement self-reports in accountability systems, but the evidence remains observational and reflects concurrent associations rather than causal impacts.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 (15-year-olds) — country-level stability across waves (PISA 2003 vs PISA 2012)
main_findings.target_variable: Country-level stability of PSEC indicators over time
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 2: absolute correlations between country averages in PISA 2003 vs 2012. Examples: inconsistency r=0.897 (absolute), non-differentiation r=0.845, non-response r=0.282, performance decline r=0.405. Rank correlations are also high for most indicators (e.g., inconsistency rank correlation 0.88; non-response rank correlation 0.525).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2003 and PISA 2012 the study leveraged country-average PSEC indicators to assess stability over time, finding that most behavioural and self-reported measures show high absolute and rank correlations across waves (generally >0.7), while non-response and performance decline show weaker stability. This indicates that behavioural PSEC monitoring can support longitudinal benchmarking at the system level, though some indicators may be more sensitive to administration or measurement conditions.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2000/2003 (15-year-olds) linked to follow-up studies — Denmark (PISA 2000→PIAAC 2012), Switzerland (PISA 2000→TREE 2010), Australia (PISA 2003→LSAY 2013), Canada (PISA 2000→YITS 2010)
main_findings.target_variable: University completion by age 25 (binary outcome) predicted by PSEC indicators
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 4: linear probability model coefficients (b) and adjusted R-squared by country. Performance decline: university b≈−0.066 (Denmark, not significant), −0.074*** (Switzerland), −0.070* (Australia), −0.132*** (Canada). Inconsistency: university b≈−0.012 (Denmark), −0.031* (Switzerland), 0.011 (Australia), −0.025* (Canada). Non-response: university b≈−0.050* (Denmark), −0.072*** (Switzerland), −0.014 (Australia), −0.034 (Canada). Adjusted R-squared for university models ranges roughly from 0.108 to 0.206 depending on country/indicator.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using linked PISA follow-up data for Denmark, Switzerland, Australia, and Canada, the study leveraged behavioural PSEC indicators (especially performance decline) to predict university completion by age 25, finding that performance decline was significantly associated with lower university completion in three of four countries and that several questionnaire-based indicators also showed country-specific predictive links. This indicates that incorporating behavioural engagement measures into early benchmarking could improve identification of students at risk of later educational non-completion, while causality cannot be inferred from these observational longitudinal associations.

data.outcome_summary: This study develops a validity argument for behavioural measures of socio-emotional and motivational skills (PSEC) using PISA microdata, with most analyses based on PISA 2012 and robustness/stability checks using PISA 2003. The authors construct multiple self-reported and behavioural indicators (e.g., perseverance/effort from questionnaires; item non-response, inconsistency, non-differentiation; and test-based performance decline and response-time effort from computer-based logs in a subset of countries). Across PISA 2012 domains (reading, mathematics, science, and collaborative problem-solving), all PSEC indicators show negative associations with contemporaneous achievement, with item non-response and test-based performance decline/response-time effort among the strongest. Country-level stability between PISA 2003 and 2012 is generally high (e.g., inconsistency r≈0.897), and longitudinal predictive validity is demonstrated in linked follow-ups for Denmark, Switzerland, Australia, and Canada (e.g., performance decline predicting university completion with b≈−0.074*** to −0.132***). The paper is correlational (no ML prediction pipeline) and does not report a PV strategy because outcomes are behavioural indicators and attainment outcomes rather than PV-based achievement scores.
